extracted.intended_audience: CRTC officials, Commissioners, broadcasting applicants and interveners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommendations on how the CRTC should process broadcasting and telecommunications licence applications, organize and run public hearings, and reduce delays in decision-making. Covers criteria for categorizing applications, briefing Commissioners, hearing format, delegation, and procedural timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearing vs non-appearing application criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish applications that must 'appear' at a public hearing from those that may be placed on the 'non-appearing' side based on significance and the likelihood of raising policy issues or serious complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-appearing examples: matters where licensees have been performing satisfactorily and there are no serious complaints, changes of a transmitter site, additions of channels to cable systems that do not raise policy issues, routine increases in cable rates, creation of limited networks (e.g., seasonal sports broadcasts), addition of small territories to authorized service areas. Appearing examples: change of control of an undertaking, significant change in programming format, renewal applications with serious programming complaints, applications for substantial increases or changes in rate structure, addition of distant television or radio channels that might hurt local stations' financial viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing (factum) book contents for Commissioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a factum book to assist Commissioners designated for a hearing containing concise, relevant material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book should contain summaries of the applications, licensing histories, comments from various branches that may raise issues (financing, programming, ownership), suggested questions Commissioners may ask applicants, and references to any relevant regulations or policy statements. Commissioners rely primarily on the factum book and also receive an oral briefing from the public hearing secretary the day before the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing format: informal debate procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an informal hearing format similar to a debate for broadcasting matters, allowing applicants and interveners to make oral presentations and respond to Commissioners' questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants speak to their applications and are questioned by Commissioners and Commission Counsel; interveners make oral presentations and are similarly questioned; applicants are permitted a reply. Evidence is not sworn, there is no cross-examination beyond Commission questioning, evidence is not 'led' by applicant counsel, and parties generally read oral submissions from prepared texts. Exception: departure from this format (including cross-examination) is rare and appropriate where precision and testing of facts are critical (e.g., revocation or non-renewal hearings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and regional hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize hearing panels and locations to balance expertise, workload, and public accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although law permits hearings chaired by as few as two members (one full-time), practice has used larger panels for significant matters (sometimes nine or ten), but more numerous hearings have led to panels rarely exceeding three or four unless major policy issues are involved. The Commission tries to organize hearings regionally so matters heard relate primarily to local undertakings; part-time members representing the province where the hearing is held are important participants and may sometimes chair panels despite lacking final-vote power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-hearing process, memos and decision timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: After hearings, staff prepare and circulate documentation and recommendations leading to Commission and Executive Committee decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically only a hearing secretary, legal counsel, and a specialist attend hearings outside Ottawa; other staff audit proceedings remotely and make notes. Upon return, the hearing secretary prepares a memorandum of comments and recommendations circulated to panel members; panel members use this in discussions and to determine recommendations to the full Commission. The Executive Committee later makes final decisions. Normally there is roughly a three-month period between hearing and announcement of a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce volume of licence amendment applications by redesigning licence content
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize routine amendment filings by removing unnecessary detailed information from licences and covering operational details in regulations instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cable licence amendment applications concern minor technical changes (channel additions, channel alignment variations, small territory additions). Rather than treating these as formal 'amendments' requiring statutory notice and possible hearings, eliminate detailed operational specifics from the licence form and cover such matters in cable regulations. Maintain administrative records via a requirement to notify the Commission of proposed changes and effective dates; notice period should allow Commission response if changes contradict regulations. The Commission has begun removing specific channel details from cable licences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of summary/file-only procedures to reduce public hearing items
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide certain types of licence amendment applications on the basis of written representations only, where they are not seriously contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a summary process (e.g., 60-day target for decisions) for certain cable licence amendment categories and other routine amendments, based on written submissions only, provided applications are not seriously contested. If decisions are made on written material, procedures must ensure applicants know of and have an opportunity to address all Commission concerns. Ground rules should be clearly articulated; vetting with CRTC staff before filing and putting applicants/interveners on notice of unexpected Commission concerns are recommended to preserve fairness and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorten lead time by publishing tentative notices concurrently with vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the pre-hearing vetting and notice timeline by running the public notice period concurrently with staff analysis and deficiency resolution, except in competitive/confidential cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish a tentative notice immediately after filing so the public has earlier access to the file. Proposed timeline example: set hearings about ten weeks after notice publication, with the intervention cutoff three weeks before the hearing, giving interveners 49 days to prepare (vs minimum 30 currently). Allow six weeks for staff analysis and deficiency letter process, leaving one week for interveners to amend based on new information. Require the Commission to decide within about three weeks between intervention cutoff and scheduled hearing whether a hearing is necessary. Withdraw applications from the hearing agenda if applicants fail to answer deficiency letters by due dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure application completeness via updated forms and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce reliance on the deficiency letter process by updating and standardizing application forms and issuing informal guidelines for common amendment types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where application forms are outdated or missing (e.g., transfers of control, amendments), applicants often omit required information leading to delays. Revise application forms (as done for new AM/FM licences) to include necessary programming and supporting information, prepare standard forms for common amendment types (e.g., cable rate increases), and publish guidelines to inform licensees of required information so fewer deficiency letters are needed and vetting lead time is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing policy development with licensing hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applications raise significant policy issues, postpone hearings until an appropriate policy framework exists to judge the merits consistently and fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using individual applications to develop general policy can produce unsatisfactory, unstructured results and make it difficult for applicants to shape submissions. Prefer postponing hearings that raise significant policy issues until policy positions are developed. Assign Commissioners (with staff support) to prepare policy papers in specific subject areas so smaller hearing panels have clearer guidance and the industry/public know the principles guiding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate routine functions to committees and senior staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve efficiency by delegating certain review, scheduling, and decision-making functions to standing committees, small panels, and empowered staff officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions (e.g., CRTC Act sections) permit committees to decide tariff and cable rate matters; the Commission has established a Tariff Committee and a cable rate coordination committee. Standing committees can oversee agenda-setting, scheduling, deciding some applications, and research. Consider delegating additional hearing responsibilities to senior staff (as allowed under other statutes) such as appointing hearing officers to conduct inquiries, hold pre-hearing conferences, sit on regional panels, act as taxing officers, and make reports. Committee effectiveness depends on Commissioners' availability for meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination policy and limits of the informal format
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize trade-offs of the informal debate format: it encourages public participation but limits adversarial testing of evidence and detail-oriented challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The informal format encourages public input and allows the Commission to hear many applications without strict courtroom procedures, but typically parties adverse in interest are not permitted to cross-examine each other, questioning is mainly by Commissioners/Commission Counsel and tends to clarify rather than discredit. Resulting problems include conflicting statements left unchallenged, lack of depth, and questioning that is general and random rather than specific. Cross-examination and more adversarial procedures should be used in circumstances where precision and testing of facts are necessary (e.g., license revocation or non-renewal).
